text: You've read an English sentence up to one hidden character. With yes or no questions, how many do you need on average? The natural answer is five. Each answer halves what's left, and five havings take 27 to 1. The ideal is log base 2 of 27, 4.75. In 1951, Claude Shannon put the true figure at about 1. No compressor beats it on average, and guessing what comes next is how language models are trained. So where do four of every five questions go? Z costs as much as E, yet E turns up 130 times as often. Instead, split the probability, not the alphabet. Is it a space, E, T, A, or O? That's nearly half. E starts near a tenth. Each ideal answer keeps half the probability, so E's share doubles. 3.3 doublings fill the bar. Z 1 in 1260 needs 10.3. A character with probability P needs K questions, where P times 2 to the K equals 1. So 2 to the K equals 1 over P, and K equals log base 2 of 1 over P. Now make each character's cost its height. The widths add to 1, so the area is the average cost. Pour the skyline flat, and its height is that average. Shannon called it entropy in bits, 1 bit per yes or no answer. For English letters, 4.11. That beats 4 but it 4 times Shannon estimate It ignores what came before What comes after a Q It U 98 times and 100 U swallows the bar, and the average falls to .16 bits. After TH, E takes two-thirds of the bar and costs about half a question. Half a question sounds impossible, but a compressor asks about long runs of letters and the fractions add up. Five questions for these three, not six. After th, it averages 1.7. But averaged over every two-letter context, it's still 2.8. Hundred-letter contexts need more text than any corpus holds, so Shannon used a predictor that knows English, a person. His subject read a passage letter by letter, guessing each next one until right. 79 of 102 on the first guess. A twin guessing the same way could rebuild the passage from these counts. Treat each count as a symbol. The same skyline pours flat at about 1.4 bits. A better guesser could only lower it. With 100 letters of context, Shannon's tests put English between 0.6 and 1.3 bits. In 2023, a language model compressing part of a book that reached Project Gutenberg after its training needed .84 bits, inside that range.
